title: Myrrha
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The nurse gets the secret out of the girl by threat and by coaxing, and promises to serve it. While the queen is away at the nine nights of Ceres' rite and the royal bed stands empty, she brings Myrrha to Cinyras under a false name, and brings her back on the nights that follow, until a light is brought in and he sees both the crime and his daughter. Myrrha runs, wanders as far as the incense country, and prays to be refused both life and death: she becomes the tree that carries her name, and the tree, in labour, gives up the child.

sentences.t:
Horret anus tremulasque manus annisque metuque
tendit et ante pedes supplex procumbit alumnae
et modo blanditur, modo, si non conscia fiat,
terret;
sentences.l: The old woman shudders, and stretches out hands trembling with her years and with fear, and falls down as a suppliant before the feet of her nursling, and now she coaxes, now — should she not be let into the secret — frightens her;
sentences.i: The old woman shudders; she holds out hands that shake with age and with fear, throws herself down as a suppliant at her nursling's feet, and coaxes her one moment and frightens her the next, if she is not let into the secret;
sentences.n: The two ablatives annis and metu hang on tremulas, “trembling with”, not on tendit: it is the hands that shake, from age and from fear together. In si non conscia fiat, conscia is nominative and belongs to the nurse — “if she should not be made a sharer”, that is, if the girl will not tell her. Modo … modo, “now … now”, sets the coaxing and the frightening alternating. Alumna is the word for a girl a nurse has suckled; here it is the poem's word, and at 442 it is the nurse's own.

sentences.t:
et indicium laquei coeptaeque minatur
mortis et officium commisso spondet amori.
sentences.l: and she threatens the laying of information about the noose and about the death begun, and pledges her service to the love — once it is entrusted to her.
sentences.i: and threatens to tell of the noose and of the death already attempted, and pledges her help to the love, if only it is confided to her.
sentences.n: Indicium is the informer's word: the disclosure a witness lays before others, and minatur takes it as its object. Coeptae, “begun”, points back before this part opens — the attempt on her own life is already made, and the noose is evidence of it. Commisso amori is dative with spondet, and the participle carries a condition inside it: “to the love, once it has been handed over to me.” Threat and bargain arrive in one sentence.

sentences.t:
Extulit illa caput lacrimisque implevit obortis
pectora nutricis; conataque saepe fateri
saepe tenet vocem,
sentences.l: She lifted her head and filled the nurse's breast with tears that had welled up; and having often tried to confess, as often she holds her voice back,
sentences.i: She raised her head, and the tears that started up filled the old woman's breast; time and again she set herself to confess, and time and again checked her voice,
sentences.n: Obortis and conata are both perfect participles of deponent verbs, oborior and conor, so both are active in force: “having welled up”, “having tried”. Lacrimis obortis is the ablative of means with implevit, not an ablative absolute. The tenses shift under the sentence: extulit and implevit are perfect, tenet present, and the present holds the repeated failure open.

sentences.t:
pudibundaque vestibus ora
texit et “o” dixit “felicem coniuge matrem!”
Hactenus, et gemuit.
sentences.l: and covered her shame-struck face with her clothes and said “O mother, happy in her husband!” This far, and she groaned.
sentences.i: and hid her burning face in her clothes and said: “Oh, my mother — happy in her husband!” No further; and she groaned.
sentences.n: Ora is the poetic plural for the single face, and pudibunda means feeling shame, not causing it. Felicem … matrem with no verb is the accusative of exclamation, the ordinary Latin way of crying out about a person; coniuge is ablative, “in respect of her husband”. The words would do for any admiring daughter; what makes them what they are is that the husband envied is the speaker's father. Hactenus, “thus far”, is an adverb standing as a whole sentence: the poem breaks off exactly where she does.

sentences.t:
Gelidus nutricis in artus
ossaque (sensit enim) penetrat tremor, albaque toto
vertice canities rigidis stetit hirta capillis.
sentences.l: An icy shudder goes into the nurse's limbs and bones — for she had understood — and the white hoariness stood bristling over her whole crown with stiffened hairs.
sentences.i: An icy shudder ran through the nurse's limbs and bones — she had understood — and over her whole scalp the white hair stood up bristling and stiff.
sentences.n: Gelidus stands at the head of its clause in 423 and its noun tremor does not arrive until 424, with the limbs and bones set between them. Sensit enim is a parenthesis and is the whole explanation of the shudder: she has taken the meaning. Canities is the abstract noun, “whiteness”, used for the white hair itself, with hirta, “shaggy, bristling”, agreeing with it; rigidis capillis is ablative, the stiffened hairs it stands up in.

sentences.t:
Multaque, ut excuteret diros, si posset, amores,
addidit:
sentences.l: And she added much, so as to shake the dreadful love out, if she could:
sentences.i: And she added a great deal more, to shake that dreadful love out of her, if she could:
sentences.n: Multa is neuter plural, “many things”, of things said. Excutere is to shake something out as one shakes dust from a cloak, and the metaphor is physical: the love is treated as a thing lodged in her. Amores is the poetic plural for the one love, and dirus carries ill omen as well as dread: the love is not only frightful but accursed. Si posset is imperfect subjunctive — the mood by attraction to the purpose clause it stands inside, the tense by secondary sequence after addidit.

sentences.t:
at virgo scit se non falsa moneri,
certa mori tamen est, si non potiatur amore.
sentences.l: but the girl knows that she is not being warned with falsehoods; still she is resolved to die, if she does not gain possession of her love.
sentences.i: But the girl knows the warning is not false; still she is set on dying if she cannot have what she loves.
sentences.n: Moneo takes an internal accusative of the thing warned, and the passive keeps it: non falsa moneri, “to be warned no false things”. Certa with the infinitive mori is “resolved to die”. Potior governs the ablative, amore; the subjunctive potiatur reports the condition as she herself frames it, not as the narrator's own.

sentences.t: “Vive,” ait haec “potiere tuo” —
sentences.l: “Live,” this one says, “you shall gain your own—”
sentences.i: “Live,” she says; “you shall have your own—”
sentences.n: Potiere is the alternative second-person singular future of potior, the same as potieris, and it governs the ablative tuo. But tuo is an adjective with no noun: the word it waits for is not spoken, and the next unit says why. Haec, “this one”, keeps the nurse distinct from the girl without naming either.

sentences.t:
et, non ausa “parente”
dicere, conticuit promissaque numine firmat.
sentences.l: and, not having dared to say “father,” she fell silent, and makes her promise firm by a divine power.
sentences.i: and, not daring to say “father,” she broke off, and binds her promise with an oath by heaven.
sentences.n: Ausa is the perfect participle of audeo, which is semi-deponent, so it is active in force: “not having dared”. Parente is the ablative tuo was waiting for, still inside line 429 with it, and Ovid prints it as a quoted word rather than as spoken: the reader is given exactly what the nurse would not say. Numine is ablative of means, the divinity by which the promise is sworn fast; conticuit is perfect and firmat present, side by side.

sentences.t:
Festa piae Cereris celebrabant annua matres
illa,
sentences.l: The matrons were keeping those yearly festivals of holy Ceres,
sentences.i: The married women were keeping that annual festival of holy Ceres —
sentences.n: Festa annua is neuter plural for the one festival, and illa is held back to the head of the next line, so that the noun and its demonstrative straddle the line-end. Pius of a deity is not “pious” in the English sense: it names the goddess's own faithfulness and the bond of duty she presides over. Matres are married women of citizen standing, the class of worshipper this rite belongs to.

sentences.t:
quibus nivea velatae corpora veste
primitias frugum dant spicea serta suarum
perque novem noctes venerem tactusque viriles
in vetitis numerant.
sentences.l: at which, veiled as to their bodies in snow-white cloth, they give wreaths of grain-ears as the first-fruits of their own harvests, and for nine nights count love-making and the touches of men among things forbidden.
sentences.i: at which, their bodies veiled in white, they offer wreaths of wheat-ears as the first-fruits of their own crops, and for nine nights reckon love-making and a man's touch among the forbidden things.
sentences.n: Velatae corpora is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle — “veiled as to their bodies” — a construction borrowed from Greek that Ovid uses constantly; the accusative names the part affected. Spicea serta is the object of dant and primitias stands in apposition to it, “garlands of ears, as first-fruits”; suarum reaches back over three words to frugum. Venus is the goddess's name used for the act itself. In vetitis is “among forbidden things”, the participle of veto used as a noun. This nine-night abstinence is what empties the king's bed at 437.

sentences.t:
Turba Cenchreis in illa
regis adest coniunx, arcanaque sacra frequentat.
sentences.l: In that throng Cenchreis, the king's wife, is present, and attends the secret rites.
sentences.i: In that crowd Cenchreis is there, the king's wife, keeping the rites no man may see.
sentences.n: Cenchreis is nominative, a Greek name, with regis coniunx in apposition: the queen, and — by the girl's own words at 422 — her mother. Frequentare is to attend in company and to keep up regularly, both at once. Arcana sacra are rites closed to outsiders; the secrecy is the rite's, and it is about to serve another one.

sentences.t:
Ergo legitima vacuus dum coniuge lectus,
nacta gravem vino Cinyram male sedula nutrix,
nomine mentito veros exponit amores
et faciem laudat.
sentences.l: So, while the bed stands empty of the lawful wife, the nurse — busy to bad purpose — having lighted on Cinyras heavy with wine, sets out a real love under a falsified name, and praises the face.
sentences.i: So, while the bed stood empty of his lawful wife, the nurse, diligent to no good end, found Cinyras heavy with wine, set out a real passion under a false name, and praised the girl's looks.
sentences.n: Vacuus takes an ablative of separation, legitima coniuge, “empty of the lawful wife”; the verb est is left out of the dum-clause. Nacta is the perfect participle of the deponent nanciscor, active in force, “having come upon”. Male sedula is a whole judgement in two words: male does not deny the diligence but condemns it — she is busy, and the busyness is the trouble. Nomine mentito is an ablative absolute — and mentior, though deponent, has its perfect participle used passively here, “the name being falsified”. Veros amores is the point of the whole deception: everything she reports is true except the name.

sentences.t:
Quaesitis virginis annis
“par” ait “est Myrrhae.”
sentences.l: The girl's years having been asked after, “She is,” she says, “a match for Myrrha.”
sentences.i: When he asked how old the girl was: “She is,” she says, “of an age with Myrrha.”
sentences.n: Quaesitis annis is an ablative absolute doing the work of a temporal clause with a change of subject: the asking is his, the answer hers. Par takes the dative, Myrrhae, “equal to Myrrha” — equal in years, and the sentence says no more than that. Not one word of the answer is false, which is how the deception works.

sentences.t:
Quam postquam adducere iussa est
utque domum rediit, “gaude mea” dixit “alumna:
vicimus.”
sentences.l: And after she was ordered to bring her, and when she had come home, “Rejoice, my nursling,” she said: “we have won.”
sentences.i: And when she had been told to bring the girl, and had got home again, she said: “Rejoice, my child — we have won.”
sentences.n: Quam is a connecting relative — “and her” — carrying Myrrha over as the object of adducere; Latin very often opens a sentence with a relative where English starts a fresh one, and you will meet it again at 499 and 513. Iussa est is passive with the infinitive dependent on it. Vicimus, first person plural, puts the nurse inside the act she has arranged.

sentences.t:
Infelix non toto pectore sentit
laetitiam virgo, praesagaque pectora maerent;
sentences.l: The unhappy girl does not feel the gladness with her whole breast, and her foreknowing heart mourns;
sentences.i: The unhappy girl does not feel that gladness with her whole heart: her heart is full of foreboding, and grieves;
sentences.n: Pectore and pectora fall within a line and a half of each other, singular then poetic plural: the first is the breast she does not wholly feel with, the second is what mourns. Praesagus is “sensing beforehand”, of a mind that knows what is coming without being told. Infelix stands at the head of the clause and its noun virgo comes only after the object laetitiam.

sentences.t: sed tamen et gaudet: tanta est discordia mentis.
sentences.l: but even so she is glad as well: so great is the discord of her mind.
sentences.i: and yet she is glad too — so far at odds with itself is her mind.
sentences.n: Et here is etiam, “as well”, not the connective. Tanta … discordia: the colon makes the second clause the explanation of the first, and discordia is the word for civil strife and for instruments out of tune. The line is the summary the narrative has been building toward, and it is the last thing said of her before the night begins.

sentences.t:
Tempus erat, quo cuncta silent, interque triones
flexerat obliquo plaustrum temone Bootes:
ad facinus venit illa suum.
sentences.l: It was the time at which all things fall silent, and Bootes had swung his wagon round between the Oxen with the pole aslant: she comes to her own deed.
sentences.i: It was the hour when everything is still, and Boötes had wheeled his wain, its pole aslant, between the Oxen: she comes to her own deed.
sentences.n: Silent is present inside a past frame, because what it states is always true. Triones are the plough-oxen, the stars of the Great Bear — the word behind septemtriones, the north — and plaustrum is the same group seen as a wagon, with Bootes as the driver behind it; the tilt of the pole is how far the night has run. Facinus is a deed of the worst kind, and suum is held back to the end of its clause: her own. The poem's other word for what she is doing, scelus, arrives at 460.

sentences.t:
Fugit aurea caelo
luna, tegunt nigrae latitantia sidera nubes:
nox caret igne suo.
sentences.l: The golden moon flees from the sky, black clouds cover the stars as they hide themselves: the night is without its own fire.
sentences.i: The golden moon flees the sky; black clouds cover the stars where they hide: night is left without her fires.
sentences.n: Caelo is a bare ablative of separation, “from the sky”, with no preposition. Latitantia is the frequentative of lateo, so the stars are made to do the hiding rather than merely to be hidden. Careo governs the ablative igne. Three clauses stand in a row with no connective between any of them: the moon goes, then the stars, and the third states what is left — a night without a fire of its own.

sentences.t:
Primus tegis, Icare, vultus
Erigoneque pio sacrata parentis amore.
sentences.l: You are the first to cover your face, Icarus, and Erigone, hallowed by dutiful love of a father.
sentences.i: You cover your face first, Icarus — and Erigone, made holy by her faithful love of a father.
sentences.n: Apostrophe: the poem turns aside to address a constellation directly, and the verb goes into the second person, with primus nominative, agreeing with the one spoken to. This is Icarius of Attica, father of Erigone, not the boy who flew; the two were set among the stars, and Bootes, named just above at 447, is identified with him — so the sky already described is now made to hide its face. Erigone is nominative and simply added to a second-person verb, without a new one of her own. Parentis is objective genitive, “love for a parent” — the love a daughter owes a father, named at the moment the poem's other daughter is going to her father's bed.

sentences.t:
Ter pedis offensi signo est revocata, ter omen
funereus bubo letali carmine fecit:
sentences.l: Three times she was called back by the sign of a foot struck, three times the funereal owl made an omen with its deadly song:
sentences.i: Three times a stumble called her back; three times the funeral owl gave its omen in a song of death:
sentences.n: Pedis offensi is a genitive of definition: the sign that consists in a stumble. Tripping as one sets out is a standard Roman omen, and revocata takes it as a summons — she was “called back”. Bubo is the eagle-owl, the bird of funerals; carmen is used of a bird's cry, here letali, deadly. Ter … ter is the ritual number, and the repetition is the point: the warning is given the full three times.

sentences.t: it tamen, et tenebrae minuunt noxque atra pudorem;
sentences.l: she goes even so, and the shadows and the black night lessen her shame;
sentences.i: still she goes, and the dark and the black night make her shame less;
sentences.n: It is the third person singular of eo, one syllable carrying the whole decision, and tamen sets it against the three omens. Minuunt has two subjects, tenebrae and nox, one on each side of it. Pudor is both the sense of shame and the shame itself; the dark does not take it away, only makes it smaller.

sentences.t:
nutricisque manum laeva tenet, altera motu
caecum iter explorat.
sentences.l: and with her left she holds the nurse's hand, with the other she searches out the blind road by movement.
sentences.i: with her left hand she holds the nurse's, and with the other feels out the unseen way.
sentences.n: Laeva and altera are ablatives with manu understood from the manum just used, “with the left hand, with the other”. Caecum iter is a transferred epithet: the road is called blind because of what the traveller cannot see on it, and the same transfer returns at 476 with caecae … noctis. Motu is ablative of means — the groping movement of the free hand.

sentences.t:
Thalami iam limina tangit,
iamque fores aperit, iam ducitur intus:
sentences.l: Now she touches the threshold of the chamber, and now she opens the doors, now she is led inside:
sentences.i: Now she is at the chamber's threshold; now she opens the door; now she is being led inside:
sentences.n: Three clauses each opening with iam, so that the approach is counted step by step. The first two verbs are hers and active; the third, ducitur, is passive — the last stage is not her own doing. Thalamus is the marriage chamber specifically, and it is the word the poem keeps for this room (again at 469). Limina and fores are plural for the one doorway.

sentences.t:
at illi
poplite succiduo genua intremuere, fugitque
et color et sanguis, animusque relinquit euntem.
sentences.l: but her knees shook, the joint giving way beneath, and both colour and blood fled, and her spirit leaves her as she goes.
sentences.i: but her knees gave under her and shook; the colour fled, and the blood with it, and her senses left her as she walked.
sentences.n: Illi is a dative of possession with genua, “the knees to her”, where English says “her knees”. Poplite succiduo is an ablative absolute, the hollow of the knee sinking. Intremuere is the poetic third-plural perfect for intremuerunt, a form you will meet all through this poem — habuere at 489 and unxere at 514 are the same. Fugit is singular although et … et joins two subjects, the verb agreeing with the nearer. Animus here is consciousness, what leaves in a faint, and euntem is the participle of eo, accusative, “her as she goes”.

sentences.t:
Quoque suo propior sceleri est, magis horret, et ausi
paenitet, et vellet non cognita posse reverti.
sentences.l: And the nearer she is to her own crime, the more she shudders, and she repents of what she has dared, and could wish she might turn back unrecognised.
sentences.i: And the closer she comes to her crime, the more she shudders; she repents of the thing she dared, and would wish she could go back, unknown.
sentences.n: Quoque here is not the adverb “also” but quo-que, “and by how much”: the ablative of measure of difference answered by magis, “the nearer … the more”. Watch for this — at 467 the same spelling is the plain adverb. Paenitet is impersonal, taking the accusative of the person (left out here) and the genitive of the thing: ausi is the participle of audeo used as a neuter noun, “of the deed dared”. Vellet is imperfect subjunctive, a wish that is felt and not acted on; cognita is nominative, agreeing with her — she wishes to go back with nobody knowing who came.

sentences.t:
Cunctantem longaeva manu deducit et alto
admotam lecto cum traderet “accipe,” dixit
“ista tua est, Cinyra” devotaque corpora iunxit.
sentences.l: The long-lived woman leads her by the hand as she holds back, and, when she was handing her over, brought close to the high bed, said: “Take her, that one there is yours, Cinyras,” and joined the accursed bodies.
sentences.i: The old woman leads her hesitating by the hand, and, as she gave her over at the high bed, said: “Take her, Cinyras; she is yours” — and joined the accursed bodies.
sentences.n: Longaeva, “long-lived”, stands alone as a noun for the nurse. Cunctantem and admotam are both feminine accusatives for Myrrha: one holding back, the other brought up to the bed. Cum traderet is cum with the imperfect subjunctive, the circumstance in which the words fall. Ista is the demonstrative of the second person, “that one there, by you”, and it points the girl at him. Devota is the strong word: made over to the powers below, cursed by the act itself, and the plural corpora takes in both of them under it.

sentences.t:
Accipit obsceno genitor sua viscera lecto
virgineosque metus levat hortaturque timentem.
sentences.l: The begetter receives his own flesh on the foul bed, and lightens her maiden fears, and encourages her as she is afraid.
sentences.i: The father takes his own flesh onto that unclean bed, eases a virgin's fears and speaks courage to her while she is afraid.
sentences.n: Viscera, properly the inner parts of the body, is the ordinary Latin word for one's own offspring, “his own flesh”; genitor, “the begetter”, and sua viscera put the relation and the act inside one line. Obscenus is not merely indecent but ill-omened and polluted, the standing word for what should not be seen. Levat metus and hortatur timentem are the plain language of a bridegroom with a frightened bride, and Ovid uses it unchanged.

sentences.t:
Forsitan aetatis quoque nomine “filia” dixit,
dixit et illa “pater,” sceleri ne nomina desint.
sentences.l: Perhaps, by the name belonging to her years as well, he said “daughter,” and she said “father,” so that names should not be missing from the crime.
sentences.i: Perhaps — the word fitted her age too — he said “daughter,” and she said “father,” so that the crime should not lack its names.
sentences.n: Aetatis nomine is “by the name that goes with her age”, the address an older man might use to any young woman; and quoque here is the plain adverb “also”, unlike Quoque at 460. Forsitan usually takes the subjunctive; the perfect indicative dixit lets the guess stand as flat statement. Sceleri is dative with desint, and ne desint is a negative purpose clause — a purpose that belongs to the poem rather than to either speaker: the horror is that the words of kinship are all in place.

sentences.t:
Plena patris thalamis excedit et impia diro
semina fert utero conceptaque crimina portat.
sentences.l: Full of her father she goes out from the chamber and carries unholy seed in a dreadful womb and bears the crimes she has conceived.
sentences.i: She leaves the bedchamber full of her father, carrying an unholy seed in a dreadful womb, bearing a crime conceived.
sentences.n: Plena takes the genitive patris and does double duty: filled with him, and pregnant by him. Thalamis is a poetic plural in the ablative of separation. Impia semina and concepta crimina say one thing twice, the second time in the language of guilt rather than of the body — concipio is the verb both for conceiving a child and for incurring a crime, and Ovid keeps both senses live in the one word.

sentences.t: Postera nox facinus geminat. Nec finis in illa est:
sentences.l: The following night doubles the deed. Nor is there an end in that one:
sentences.i: The next night doubles the deed. Nor does it end there:
sentences.n: Geminat is “makes twin”, and nox is its subject: the night, not the girl, is made to do the counting. Facinus is the same word as at 448, so the second night is named as exactly the first. In illa, “in that one”, refers to the night, and the colon opens onto how long it in fact went on.

sentences.t:
cum tandem Cinyras, avidus cognoscere amantem
post tot concubitus, inlato lumine vidit
et scelus et natam,
sentences.l: until at last Cinyras, greedy to know his lover after so many couplings, with a light brought in saw both the crime and his daughter,
sentences.i: until at last Cinyras, eager after so many couplings to learn who his lover was, had a light brought in and saw both the crime and his own daughter —
sentences.n: Cum tandem is the inverted cum-clause: the sentence's real event stands in the subordinate clause, with the indicative vidit. Post tot concubitus counts the acts and not the nights — a concubitus is a lying-together. Avidus takes the infinitive cognoscere, and cognoscere here is to find out who she is — the identification the false name has kept from him. Inlato lumine is an ablative absolute, “a light having been brought in”; the older spelling inl- is the edition's own and is left as printed. Et … et yokes scelus and natam under the one verb, the deed and the person seen in the same instant.

sentences.t:
verbisque dolore retentis
pendenti nitidum vagina deripit ensem.
sentences.l: and, his words held back by grief, he snatches the shining sword down from the hanging scabbard.
sentences.i: and, with grief holding back every word, he tears the bright sword from its hanging sheath.
sentences.n: Verbis … retentis is an ablative absolute with dolore as the ablative of the cause doing the holding: the grief keeps the words in, so he says nothing at all. Deripit, “tears down from”, takes the ablative of separation pendenti vagina — the scabbard hangs where it was left. Nitidum, “gleaming”, is the one detail given to the weapon, and it is given because there is now a light in the room.

sentences.t:
Myrrha fugit, tenebrisque et caecae munere noctis
intercepta neci est:
sentences.l: Myrrha flees, and by the darkness and by the gift of the blind night she was snatched away from death:
sentences.i: Myrrha runs, and the dark and the blind night's gift stole her out of death's reach:
sentences.n: Neci is a dative of disadvantage with intercepta: the killing is intercepted, cheated of her. Caecae noctis is the same transferred epithet as caecum iter at 456 — the night is called blind for what it does to those inside it, and here for once that serves her. Tenebris and munere are two coordinated ablatives naming one thing twice — the dark, and then the dark called a gift.

sentences.t:
latosque vagata per agros
palmiferos Arabas Panchaeaque rura reliquit;
sentences.l: and, having wandered over broad fields, she left the palm-bearing Arabs and the Panchaean country behind;
sentences.i: and, wandering across wide country, she left palm-bearing Arabia and the fields of Panchaia behind her;
sentences.n: Vagata is the perfect participle of the deponent vagor, active in force. Arabas is the Greek accusative plural of Arabes, the people standing for their land. Panchaia is the spice-bearing country of the far south in ancient imagining, named here because incense is where this flight is going to end. Magnus prints the perfect reliquit, “she left”; the other witness has the present relinquit, which would keep the leaving going alongside the wandering.

sentences.l: and she wandered through nine horns of the returning moon, when at last, worn out, she rested in the Sabaean land; and she was scarcely carrying her womb's burden.
sentences.i: and she wandered while the moon came back nine times to its horns, until at last, worn out, she came to rest in the land of Saba; and she could hardly carry her womb's burden.
sentences.n: Cornua lunae are the horns of the crescent, one return for each month — nine of them, the full term. Redeuntis is the present participle, of the moon in the act of coming back. Perque novem opens this line exactly as it opened 434, where the same number counted the forbidden nights of Ceres' rite. Cum tandem is again the inverted cum-clause. Terra Sabaea is a bare ablative of place, the incense country of southern Arabia; portabat is imperfect, the carrying still going on as the wandering stops.

sentences.t:
Tum nescia voti
atque inter mortisque metus et taedia vitae
est tales complexa preces:
sentences.l: Then, not knowing her own prayer, and between both fears of death and a weariness of life, she gathered such prayers as these:
sentences.i: Then, not knowing what to pray for, caught between the fear of death and the weariness of life, she framed her prayer in these words:
sentences.n: Nescia takes an objective genitive, voti: she does not know what to ask for. The -que sits on mortis but does the work of a first connective with the following et, coupling the two things inter governs — “between both … and …”. Complexa est is the deponent perfect of complector, active in force; used of words it is to gather them into one compass.

sentences.t:
“O siqua patetis
numina confessis, merui nec triste recuso
supplicium.
sentences.l: “O if there are any powers that stand open to those who confess, I have deserved it, and I do not refuse a grim punishment.
sentences.i: “O gods — if any of you stand open to those who confess — I have earned it, and I do not refuse a hard punishment.
sentences.n: After si the indefinite drops its ali-, so qua is aliqua, here the neuter plural agreeing with numina, “if any powers”. Patetis is second person because the powers are being addressed, so the conditional and the invocation are one clause. Confessis is a dative with patetis, the participle of confiteor used as a noun, “to those who have confessed”. Merui is left without an object: “I have deserved it”, with the it unnamed.

sentences.t:
Sed ne violem vivosque superstes
mortuaque exstinctos, ambobus pellite regnis
mutataeque mihi vitamque necemque negate.”
sentences.l: But so that I may not, surviving, defile the living, nor, dead, the dead, drive me out of both kingdoms, and to me, changed, refuse both life and death.”
sentences.i: But so that I may not pollute the living while I survive, nor the dead once I am dead, drive me from both kingdoms; change me, and deny me life and death alike.”
sentences.n: Superstes and mortua are nominatives agreeing with the subject of violem and doing the work of adverbial clauses, “while I survive”, “once I am dead”; they pair off with the two objects vivos and exstinctos in the same order. Ambobus regnis is an ablative of separation with pellite, the realm of the living and the realm of the dead. Mutatae mihi is the dative with negate, and the request she is really making is smuggled inside it: change me first, then refuse me both. Nex is death as something dealt, a killing, where mors would be death as a state: what she asks to be refused, alongside life, is any dispatch out of it.

sentences.t:
Numen confessis aliquod patet: ultima certe
vota suos habuere deos.
sentences.l: Some divine power does stand open to those who confess: her last prayers, at any rate, had gods of their own.
sentences.i: Some power is open to those who confess: her last prayers, at least, found gods of their own.
sentences.n: The narrator answers her with her own words — numen, patet, confessis, all three from 483 and 484 — with the si taken away and aliquod standing where her qua stood: what she could only put as a condition is said as a fact. Habuere is the poetic third-plural perfect for habuerunt, the same form as intremuere at 458. Suos deos, “gods of their own”, means gods willing to be theirs; ultima and vota stand on either side of certe.

sentences.l: For the earth comes over the legs of her as she speaks, and through her burst nails a slanting root stretches out, the stays of a long trunk;
sentences.i: For earth climbs over her legs while she is still speaking, and through the nails as they split a root spreads out sideways, the anchor of a tall trunk;
sentences.n: Loquentis is a present participle in the genitive, “of her as she speaks” — the change begins before the prayer is finished, and the participle is where that is said. Supervenit takes the accusative crura, “comes up over”. Ruptos … ungues is where the root comes out. Firmamina is a neuter plural in apposition to the single radix, “the things that make firm”, and obliqua is the root running out aslant rather than down.

sentences.t:
ossaque robur agunt, mediaque manente medulla
sanguis it in sucos, in magnos bracchia ramos,
in parvos digiti, duratur cortice pellis.
sentences.l: and the bones drive out hard wood, and, the marrow staying in the middle, the blood goes into sap, the arms into great branches, the fingers into small ones, the skin is hardened with bark.
sentences.i: her bones put out heartwood; the marrow stays where it was, and the blood turns to sap, the arms to great boughs, the fingers to small ones, and the skin hardens into bark.
sentences.n: Robur is both the hard timber of the oak and hardness itself, and agunt is the technical verb for a plant putting out root or wood — the same verb returns at 512 of the tree driving cracks. Media manente medulla is an ablative absolute: the marrow alone is unchanged, and it keeps the place it had at the centre. It, from eo, is used once and then understood with bracchia and digiti, so the verb drops away as the list runs. Duratur is passive with cortice as the means.

sentences.t:
Iamque gravem crescens uterum perstrinxerat arbor
pectoraque obruerat collumque operire parabat,
sentences.l: And already the growing tree had drawn tight about the heavy womb and had buried the breast and was preparing to cover the neck,
sentences.i: And now the growing tree had closed round the heavy womb, had buried the breast, and was making ready to cover the neck;
sentences.n: Perstringere is to bind tight around, of the wood closing on the belly; gravis is the standing word for a pregnant body, “heavy”. Two pluperfects and then an imperfect, parabat: the first two stages are done, the third is only in preparation, and that unfinished third is what leaves the next line its opening. Pectora is a poetic plural.

sentences.t:
non tulit illa moram venientique obvia ligno
subsedit mersitque suos in cortice vultus.
sentences.l: she did not bear the delay, and, going to meet the wood as it came, she settled down and sank her own face in the bark.
sentences.i: she could not bear the waiting: she went down to meet the wood as it came, and buried her face in the bark.
sentences.n: Obvia is a predicative nominative taking the dative venienti ligno, “in the way of the wood as it comes” — she moves toward the change rather than away from it. Mersit takes in with the ablative rather than the accusative: the face goes in and stays. Vultus is a poetic plural for the one face. The last thing she does of her own will is to hurry the transformation on.

sentences.t:
Quae quamquam amisit veteres cum corpore sensus,
flet tamen, et tepidae manant ex arbore guttae.
sentences.l: And she, though she lost her old feeling along with her body, weeps nonetheless, and warm drops run out of the tree.
sentences.i: And she, though she has lost her old senses along with her body, weeps still, and warm drops run from the tree.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative — “and she” — opening the sentence, as Quam did at 441. Quamquam takes the indicative, the ordinary concessive. Veteres sensus covers both the bodily senses and what she felt with them, and cum corpore ties the two together as one loss. Tepidae, “warm”, is the single word that keeps the drops human.

sentences.t:
Est honor et lacrimis, stillataque robore murra
nomen erile tenet nulloque tacebitur aevo.
sentences.l: There is honour for the tears as well, and the myrrh dripped from the hard wood keeps its mistress's name, and will be passed over in silence in no age.
sentences.i: The tears too have their honour: the myrrh that drips from the wood keeps its mistress's name, and no age will leave it unspoken.
sentences.n: Et is again etiam, “as well”. Stillata is a perfect participle with robore as ablative of source; Magnus prints robore, “from the hard wood”, where the other witness reads cortice, “from the bark” — the same drops, taken at the timber or at the surface. Erilis is the adjective of era, the mistress of a household: the resin is named after the woman it came out of, murra for Myrrha. Tacebitur is taceo in the personal passive with murra as its subject, “it will be passed over in silence”, where English has to say instead that no age will be silent about it; nullo aevo is ablative of time.

sentences.t:
At male conceptus sub robore creverat infans
quaerebatque viam, qua se genetrice relicta
exsereret: media gravidus tumet arbore venter.
sentences.l: But the child, ill conceived, had grown under the hard wood, and was seeking a way by which, its mother left behind, it might put itself out: the swollen belly bulges in the middle of the tree.
sentences.i: But the ill-conceived child had grown under the wood and was looking for a way to work itself out and leave its mother behind: the swollen belly bulges in the middle of the tree.
sentences.n: Male conceptus is the same construction as male sedula at 438: the adverb carries the whole judgement, and here it means both wrongly begotten and to no good end. Qua … exsereret is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive, “a way by which it might get itself out”, and se exsereret is reflexive. Genetrice relicta is an ablative absolute. The last clause runs adjective, adjective, verb, noun, noun — media gravidus tumet arbore venter — with each adjective reaching over the verb to its own noun, media to arbore and gravidus to venter, so that the words for the tree and the words for the belly are interlocked.

sentences.t:
Tendit onus matrem: neque habent sua verba dolores,
nec Lucina potest parientis voce vocari.
sentences.l: The burden strains the mother: and the pains do not have their own words, nor can Lucina be called with the voice of a woman giving birth.
sentences.i: The burden strains the mother, and her pangs have no words of their own, and Lucina cannot be called with a labouring woman's voice.
sentences.n: Matrem is the object of tendit: the tree is still called the mother, and the noun does not change with the shape. Sua verba are the words that belong to labour by right — the cries she now has no mouth for. Lucina is the goddess invoked at a birth, a cult title used of Juno and of Diana; here she is treated as the goddess of the birth-bed in her own person, and she arrives at 510. Parientis is the present participle of pario in the genitive, and voce is the ablative of means with the passive vocari.

sentences.t:
Nitenti tamen est similis curvataque crebros
dat gemitus arbor lacrimisque cadentibus umet.
sentences.l: Still she is like one straining, and the tree, bent over, gives thick-coming groans and is wet with falling tears.
sentences.i: Still she is like a woman in labour: the tree bends, gives groan upon groan, and is wet with falling tears.
sentences.n: Similis takes the dative, nitenti, the present participle of nitor used absolutely of the effort of childbirth, “one straining”. Curvata is bent double, and belongs equally to a tree and to a woman. Creber is “close-packed, coming thick”, and dat gemitus is the ordinary idiom for uttering a groan. Umet is intransitive, “is damp”, with lacrimis cadentibus as the ablative of cause. One subject, arbor, serves est similis, dat gemitus and umet alike; the literal says “she” for the first because the poem is still calling this the mother, as it does at 506.

sentences.t:
Constitit ad ramos mitis Lucina dolentes
admovitque manus et verba puerpera dixit.
sentences.l: Gentle Lucina took her stand at the grieving branches and moved her hands to them and said the words of childbed.
sentences.i: Kind Lucina stood by the branches in their pain, laid her hands on them, and said the words that bring a child.
sentences.n: Ramos and its adjective dolentes are pulled apart, with mitis Lucina standing between them, so that the goddess is enclosed by the branches she comes to. Dolentes gives the boughs the participle a body would have. Admovit manus is the midwife's touch. Puerpera is properly the adjective of a woman in childbed, transferred here to the words — the formula spoken to bring a delivery on.

sentences.t:
Arbor agit rimas et fissa cortice vivum
reddit onus, vagitque puer;
sentences.l: The tree drives cracks open and, split in the bark, gives back its living burden, and the boy wails;
sentences.i: The tree opens in cracks and, its bark split, gives back the living burden, and the boy cries out;
sentences.n: Agit rimas is the same verb as at 492, where the bones drove out wood: the tree does now what the body did then. Cortice is an ablative of respect with the nominative participle fissa, “cleft in its bark”. Reddit is “gives back”: what the tree returns is what the womb was carrying. Vagire is the specific verb for the cry of a newborn.

sentences.t:
quem mollibus herbis
naides impositum lacrimis unxere parentis.
sentences.l: and him, laid on soft grasses, the naiads anointed with his mother's tears.
sentences.i: and the naiads laid him on soft grass and anointed him with his mother's tears.
sentences.n: Quem is another connecting relative, “and him”. Impositum agrees with it, “having been laid on”, with mollibus herbis as the dative that the compound verb impono takes. Unxere is the poetic third-plural perfect for unxerunt. The tears are the myrrh of 500 and 501, and anointing is what myrrh is for; parentis, “of the parent”, is a word that would cover either, and here it is the mother.

sentences.t:
Laudaret faciem Livor quoque. Qualia namque
corpora nudorum tabula pinguntur Amorum,
talis erat:
sentences.l: Envy too would praise his face. For such as the bodies of naked Loves are painted on a panel, such was he:
sentences.i: Even Envy would praise his face. For the kind of body naked Loves are painted with on a panel — that was his:
sentences.n: Livor is the blue-black of a bruise and so the colour of spite, personified here and capitalised in the edition. Laudaret is a potential subjunctive, “would praise”, of something that is not in fact the case. Quoque here is the plain adverb again. Qualia … talis is the correlative pair, “of what kind … of such kind”, and the comparison shifts number as it goes: the neuter plural bodies of the painted Loves answer to the one masculine child. Tabula is the wooden panel a painting was made on, ablative of place.

sentences.t:
sed, ne faciat discrimina cultus,
aut huic adde leves, aut illi deme pharetras.
sentences.l: but, so that the outfit may not make differences, either add light quivers to this one, or take them from that one.
sentences.i: but, so that the gear makes no difference between them, either add a light quiver to the child, or take the quivers away from the painting.
sentences.n: Cultus is dress and equipment — here the quiver, the only thing that would tell the painted Loves from the child. Ne faciat is a negative purpose clause. Huic and illi are datives with adde and deme, “to this one here”, “from that one there”: the child at hand, and the figures on the panel. Magnus prints the singular illi; the other witness has the plural illis, which agrees better with the plural Amorum above. The imperatives turn to a second person and hand the correction to whoever is listening.
